articles.title: What my review gate does when Codex crashes, gets cut off or writes two verdicts
articles.excerpt: When Codex crashes, gets cut off or writes two verdicts while it reviews Claude Code's commits, my gate saves no verdict for that commit. With no saved verdict the merge check refuses the commit, so t…
articles.body: When Codex crashes, gets cut off or writes two verdicts while it reviews Claude Code's commits, my gate saves no verdict for that commit. With no saved verdict the merge check refuses the commit, so the only review that counts is a final message with exactly one valid Verdict line. two-engines-gate is the free, MIT licensed version of how I make Claude Code and Codex check each other. I wrote about the review loop , the commit hash records and the dirty working tree refusal before. The post right before this one covers what the gate does about weakened or deleted tests . This post is about the review that ends without a usable answer. Three exit codes review.sh ends in one of three ways: 0 : the reviewer answered ACCEPT, and the verdict is saved.

articles.title: Signing Netlify Webhooks with HMAC and Timestamps for a Home Automation Server
articles.excerpt: Why I Signed My Netlify Webhooks When I moved my personal site to Netlify I also wanted the same deployment to trigger a few home‑automation scripts that run on a Raspberry Pi in my garage. A simple H…
articles.body: Why I Signed My Netlify Webhooks When I moved my personal site to Netlify I also wanted the same deployment to trigger a few home‑automation scripts that run on a Raspberry Pi in my garage. A simple HTTP POST would work, but anyone who discovers the endpoint could fire my scripts at will. The solution I settled on is a classic HMAC signature plus a short‑lived timestamp. It’s cheap, stateless, and works well with the serverless functions Netlify provides. The Core Idea Shared secret – a random string known only to the Netlify site and my home server. HMAC‑SHA256 – the payload (or a deterministic string) is signed with the secret. Timestamp – added to the request and validated to prevent replay attacks. When the request arrives, the server recomputes the HMAC and compares it to the header.

articles.title: leantext: up to 99% fewer tokens when your coding agent reads the web
articles.excerpt: Your coding agent opens a docs page to answer one question. It gets the navigation bar, the sidebar, the footer, hidden menus, scripts and markup. Somewhere in there is the answer, and you pay for all…
articles.body: Your coding agent opens a docs page to answer one question. It gets the navigation bar, the sidebar, the footer, hidden menus, scripts and markup. Somewhere in there is the answer, and you pay for all of it, in tokens, in context window and in latency. On PyPI's NumPy page, the project description is about 2,000 tokens. The whole page, converted to Markdown the usual way, is 92,348. Most of it is a hidden list of every file in every release, with hashes, that you never see in a browser. leantext removes that noise before it reaches your agent, checks that nothing important went with it, and tells you what it saved. https://github.com/shouvik12/leantext What it does Point it at a URL or a file. Markdown comes out on stdout.

articles.title: Your CI failed. Was it a flake or a real break?
articles.excerpt: Your CI failed. Was it a flake or a real break? Last week I watched a team re-run a red CI job three times, merge on the third green run, and ship the bug anyway. The test was not flaky. The retry jus…
articles.body: Your CI failed. Was it a flake or a real break? Last week I watched a team re-run a red CI job three times, merge on the third green run, and ship the bug anyway. The test was not flaky. The retry just hid it for one run. The opposite happens just as often: a genuinely flaky test blocks a good PR for an afternoon while someone scrolls a 40,000-line log looking for the first real error. I built a small step that answers three questions before anyone re-runs anything: Where did it actually break first? Is each failing test flaky, or genuinely broken? Has this exact failure happened before? It is called CI Failure Detective , and it runs entirely inside your runner. No log ever leaves your repo. No signup, no server, no bill.

articles.excerpt: An AI phone agent that sounds great in a demo can still fail on the one call that matters: the angry customer, the emergency, the caller who asks something it was never told. You only find out which k…
articles.body: An AI phone agent that sounds great in a demo can still fail on the one call that matters: the angry customer, the emergency, the caller who asks something it was never told. You only find out which kind you have by testing it on purpose, before your customers do it for you. This is how we test every agent before it goes live. The results are public: you can see the latest run on our agent QA console . Why a few test calls are not enough Language models are not deterministic. The same question can get a slightly different answer each time. So an agent that handled your three test calls perfectly can still mishandle the fourth.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

articles.body: NASA just gave us our best look yet at its Artemis III moon-lander test flight. The agency laid out a detailed concept of operations for Artemis III today (Oct. 23) during a press conference at Kennedy Space Center , stressing how important the flight is to its moon plans and how challenging it will be to make everything go right. "We're launching three of the most powerful rockets in the world, and undertaking what is likely the most complicated launch campaign ever undertaken," Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, said during today's event, which lasted more than two hours. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 23, 2007: NASA launches Harmony module to ISS on STS-120 space shuttle mission
articles.excerpt: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station . The Harmony module is a utility hub 14 feet wide and 24 feet long, or about the length of a minibus. It joins the European Space Agency's Columbus module and Japan's Kibo laboratory and serves as the crew quarters for the American astronauts. Once it was installed, the space station grew from about the size of a three-bedroom house to something more like a five-bedroom house. When astronauts delivered Harmony to the space station , they left it temporarily attached to the Unity node. After the shuttle left, astronauts used the space station's robotic arm to move the shuttle docking port out of the way at the Destiny module.
